name: The Reckoning Table
goal: Evaluate an expression by hand and predict its type and value before running it.

description.what: How Python turns a piece of arithmetic into a single value: which operators exist, the order they are applied in, what the two division operators really do, how one type becomes another, and why `=` and `==` are different instructions.
description.why: An expression that is merely misread does not crash - it produces a confident wrong number, and a program that prints the wrong answer without complaining is far harder to catch than one that stops.
description.enables: You will be able to look at a line of arithmetic and say what value and what type it produces before you run it, choose between `/` and `//` on purpose, convert between text and numbers deliberately, and update a stored value without writing its name twice.
description.assumes: Only the two floors below: that a program runs top to bottom, that `print` shows a value, that a name can be pointed at a value, and that a line typed by a person arrives as text.
description.assessed: You will predict output and types before running anything, track a value through a run of updates, repair programs that are silently wrong rather than broken, and write short programs that read typed numbers and print exact answers.

sections.title: An expression is a recipe that becomes a value
sections.body:
An **expression** is any piece of source code that Python works out into a single value. `7` is an expression, and so is `3 + 4`, and so is `price * 2 - discount`. Python does not keep the recipe: it evaluates it, gets one value, and that value is what the rest of the line sees.

The arithmetic operators are `+` for addition, `-` for subtraction, `*` for multiplication, `/` for division, `//` for whole-number division, `%` for the amount left over, and `**` for raising to a power. The last three are the ones nobody guesses correctly the first time, and they are the ones this floor drills.

`%` deserves a sentence of its own, because it is not a percent sign here. `17 % 5` is `2` - the amount left after taking out as many whole fives as will fit. Together `//` and `%` answer the two halves of a sharing-out question: how many each, and how many over.

The habit this whole floor is built on is this: before you run anything, say what you expect the answer to be. Being wrong on paper costs nothing and shows you exactly where your model of the language is broken, which is the only thing that ever fixes it.

annotations.text: The simplest expression with an operator in it: two values and one operator become the single value 7.
`//` asks how many whole fives fit inside seventeen. Three do, so it answers 3 rather than 3.4.
`%` asks what is left once those three fives are taken out, which is 2. Seventeen is 5 * 3 + 2.
`**` is a power, not a repeated star: two multiplied by itself ten times, which is 1024.

checkpoint.prompt: Predict all three lines before you run it. What does this program print?
checkpoint.explain: The first line catches anybody working right to left: `7 - 2 - 1` groups as `(7 - 2) - 1`, which is 4, rather than `7 - (2 - 1)`, which would be 6. The third is a power and not three times two, so it is 9 - `**` is the operator most often read as multiplication at a glance.

sections.title: Order of evaluation, and why 2 + 3 * 4 is not 20
sections.body:
Python does not read an expression strictly left to right. It applies operators in a fixed order of **precedence**: powers first, then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%`, then `+` and `-` last. So `2 + 3 * 4` multiplies before it adds and gives `14`. Reading it as twenty is reading it as a person, not as Python.

When two operators sit at the same level, Python works left to right, which is why `10 - 4 - 3` is 3. The single exception is `**`, which groups from the right, so `2 ** 3 ** 2` is `2 ** 9` and therefore 512.

Brackets beat everything. `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20, because the bracketed expression is worked out first and becomes one value before the multiplication ever sees it. Brackets cost nothing at run time, so write them whenever the order is not instantly obvious to a reader, including you next week.

The practical rule: when an expression mixes `+` with `*` or a division, either bracket it or be certain. Wrong precedence is a silent bug - the program runs perfectly and prints the wrong number, which is far worse than a crash.

annotations.text: `3 * 4` is worked out first and becomes 12, then 2 is added, giving 14.
The brackets force the addition to happen first, so the same four numbers give 20 instead.
`**` is the one operator that groups from the right: this is 2 ** 9, not 8 ** 2. Those differ by 448.
`//` binds tighter than `-`, so this is 20 - 3 and not 14 // 2. The answer is 17.

checkpoint.prompt: Work each line out by precedence, then say what the program prints.
checkpoint.explain: The same three numbers give 7 or 9 depending only on where the brackets are, which is the point: precedence is not a detail, it changes the answer. The third line is 12 - 2, because `//` sits at the multiplication level and runs before the subtraction - reading it left to right would give 1.

sections.title: Two kinds of division, and turning one type into another
sections.body:
`/` always produces a float, even when it divides exactly: `6 / 3` is `2.0`, not `2`. `//` throws the fraction away and gives the whole part, so `7 // 2` is `3`. Choosing the wrong one is a genuine source of wrong answers - a count of people or pages or biscuits should almost always come from `//`, because 3.5 children is not an answer to anything.

A float is catching. Mix one float into an expression and the result is a float too, so `10 // 4.0` is `2.0` rather than `2`. That is how a decimal point turns up in output nobody wanted one in.

Types never convert themselves, so you convert them on purpose: `int(x)` builds a whole number, `float(x)` builds a decimal number, `str(x)` builds text. `int("25")` is the number 25, and `int(3.9)` is `3` - it chops towards zero rather than rounding, so it is not a rounding function.

This is also why `"3" + 4` stops the program with a TypeError while `"3" * 4` happily gives `3333`. `+` between text and a number has no single agreed meaning, so Python refuses rather than guessing; `*` between text and a whole number does have one, which is repetition. To build a message out of a number, convert it first with `str`.
sections.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(6 / 3)
print(10 // 4.0)
print(int("25") + 1)
print(int(3.9))
print("3" * 4)
print("total: " + str(12))

annotations.text: True division always hands back a float, so this is 3.5.
Even a division that comes out exactly is a float: 2.0, with the point, and not 2.
One float in the expression makes the result a float, so floor division here gives 2.0.
`int` on a float chops the fraction off rather than rounding, so 3.9 becomes 3 and not 4.
`str(12)` makes the text `12`, and text joins to text with `+`. Without the `str` this line would be a TypeError.

checkpoint.prompt: Say exactly what each line prints, decimal points included.
checkpoint.explain: The first line is the trap: eight divides by four exactly, and `/` still gives `2.0`, because the operator decides the type rather than the numbers. `int(2.7)` is 2 and not 3 because converting chops rather than rounds, which is a different job with its own function.

sections.title: Updating a value, and asking whether two values are equal
sections.body:
Adding to what a name already holds is so common that it has a shorthand. `total = total + 5` can be written `total += 5`, and the same works for `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `//=` and `%=`. These are **augmented assignments**: the old value is read, the operator is applied, and the name is pointed at the answer. The name must already refer to something, because the line reads before it writes.

The augmented form keeps the type rules of its own operator, so `//=` keeps a whole number whole while `/=` turns it into a float. `count = 7` followed by `count /= 2` leaves `3.5`; with `//=` it leaves `3`.

Now the confusion that catches everybody. `=` is a command and `==` is a question. `x = 5` **makes** `x` refer to 5 and produces no value at all. `x == 5` **asks** whether `x` already refers to 5, and produces `True` or `False`.

A reliable way to keep them apart is to read them aloud differently: say **becomes** for `=` and **is equal to** for `==`. `print(x == 5)` prints a yes-or-no answer, while `print(x = 5)` is not a question, is not valid, and Python refuses the line.
sections.code:
total = 4
total += 6
print(total)
total //= 3
print(total)
count = 7
count /= 2
print(count)
print(total == 3)
print(total == 10)

annotations.text: Exactly the same as `total = total + 6`: the old 4 is read, 6 is added, and the name moves onto 10.
10 // 3 is 3, so `total` now refers to the whole number 3. Nothing here is a float.
`/=` carries the float rule of `/` with it, so `count` becomes 3.5 rather than 3.
Two equals signs, so this is a question. It prints True, and it does not change `total`.

checkpoint.prompt: Track the value under `score` line by line, then give the three printed lines.
checkpoint.explain: The last two lines ask questions and answer them; neither changes `score`, which is still 15 when the program ends. Expecting the final line to put `score` back to 10 means reading `==` as `=`, which is the commonest beginner bug there is and the reason this floor names it out loud.

guided-practice.prompt: Work each expression out by precedence before you answer. What does this program print? Give all four lines.
guided-practice.explain: Line one is the headline case of the whole floor: multiplication runs before addition, so it is 14 and never 20. Line four is the exception to left-to-right - `**` groups from the right, so it is `2 ** 9`, and reading it as `8 ** 2` gives 64 instead of 512.
guided-practice.hint: Powers first, then `*` `/` `//` `%`, then `+` and `-`. Brackets jump the queue, and `**` alone groups from the right.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete this so that it prints `5`. Use the shorthand update form for both steps rather than writing `total` twice on a line.
guided-practice.explain: The second blank must be `//=` and not `/=`, because `/=` would leave `5.0` while the prompt asks for `5`. That single character is the difference between a whole number and a float, and it is the same difference that puts an unwanted decimal point into real output.
guided-practice.hint: Four plus six is ten, and ten has to become five without gaining a decimal point.

guided-practice.prompt:
Give the value `total` refers to after each line of this program runs.

`total = 40`
`total += 5`
`total //= 6`
`total -= 1.0`
guided-practice.explain: 45 // 6 is 7 rather than 7.5, because floor division discards the fraction instead of rounding it. The last step is the one to watch: subtracting the float `1.0` makes the whole result a float, so the answer is `6.0` and not `6` - one float anywhere in an expression is enough to change the type that comes out.
guided-practice.hint: Write the running value beside each line, and watch the type as closely as the number.

guided-practice.prompt: A stopwatch has been stopped and reports a whole number of seconds, typed on one line. Write a program that prints the number of complete minutes and the number of seconds left over, on one line, separated by a single space. For the typed line `90` it prints `1 30`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
seconds = int(input())
# print the whole minutes, then the seconds left over,
# on one line separated by a single space
guided-practice.hint: `//` gives how many whole sixties fit; `%` gives what is left over. One `print` with a comma between two values puts a single space between them.
guided-practice.explain: `//` and `%` are the two halves of one question, which is why they so often appear together on the same value. Using `/` here would print `1.5 30` for the first test - a number of minutes that is true and useless, because the thing being counted cannot be half of one.

guided-practice.prompt: This program reads a number of biscuits and then a number of children, and should print how many whole biscuits each child gets. For the typed lines `7` and `2` it should print `3`, but it prints `3.5`. Repair it.
guided-practice.starterCode:
biscuits = int(input())
children = int(input())
print(biscuits / children)
guided-practice.solution:
biscuits = int(input())
children = int(input())
print(biscuits // children)
guided-practice.hint: One character has to change. Ask which of the two division operators can never produce half a biscuit.
guided-practice.explain: `/` is not wrong arithmetic - it answers the wrong question, giving how much rather than how many whole ones. The third test is what proves the fix: one biscuit between four children is `0` each, and a program printing `0.25` there has understood neither the biscuits nor the children.

guided-practice.prompt: A banner is made by repeating a word. Write a program that reads a word on the first line and a whole number of repeats on the second, then prints the word repeated that many times with nothing between the copies, and on a second line prints `repeated N times`, where `N` is the number that was typed. For the typed lines `ab` and `3` it prints `ababab` and then `repeated 3 times`.
guided-practice.starterCode:
word = input()
count = int(input())
# print the repeated word, then the sentence about it
guided-practice.solution:
word = input()
count = int(input())
print(word * count)
print("repeated " + str(count) + " times")
guided-practice.hint: Text multiplied by a whole number repeats it. To glue a number into a piece of text with `+`, convert it with `str` first.
guided-practice.explain: The same typed value is used two different ways in one program - as a number for the repetition and as text for the sentence - which is exactly why conversion is explicit in Python rather than automatic. Writing `"repeated " + count` raises a TypeError, because `+` will not guess whether you meant to add or to join.

independent-practice.prompt: A shop applies a discount. The price in whole pence is typed on the first line and the discount as a whole percentage on the second. Print the price the customer actually pays, in whole pence, with any fraction of a penny dropped in the shop's favour. For the typed lines `1000` and `10` the program prints `900`.
independent-practice.solution:
price = int(input())
percent = int(input())
print(price - price * percent // 100)
independent-practice.explain: The second test is where a careless order of operations shows up: 33 percent of 999 is 329.67, and the answer must come out as the whole number 670. Anything printing `670.0` has let a float in, and anything dividing before it multiplies loses the pence entirely, because 33 // 100 is 0.

independent-practice.prompt: A whole number of seconds is typed on one line. Print one line reading `2 minutes and 5 seconds` for the typed line `125`, with the two numbers replaced by the right ones for whatever was typed. The wording and the spacing are always the same.
independent-practice.solution:
seconds = int(input())
print(str(seconds // 60) + " minutes and " + str(seconds % 60) + " seconds")
independent-practice.explain: Both numbers have to become text before they can sit inside a sentence, and both have to be whole for the sentence to read properly - `2.0833 minutes` is not what anybody asked for. The last test is a reminder that the program was never asked to stop at sixty minutes, and inventing that rule fails it.

independent-practice.prompt: Two whole numbers are typed, one per line: the amount a customer paid and the amount they owed. Print `True` if the two amounts are the same and `False` if they are not.
independent-practice.solution:
paid = int(input())
owed = int(input())
print(paid == owed)
independent-practice.explain: The single-equals version of that line is not a slightly wrong answer, it is a syntax error, because assignment is a command and cannot sit inside a call where a value belongs. The last test matters because -3 and 3 are different amounts even though they are the same distance from nothing, and comparing numbers rather than typed text is what makes that come out right.

independent-practice.prompt: Two whole numbers are typed, one per line. Print `True` if the second one divides into parts of the first size with nothing at all left over, and `False` otherwise. For the typed lines `3` and `12` the answer is `True`; for `5` and `12` it is `False`.
independent-practice.solution:
part = int(input())
total = int(input())
print(total % part == 0)
independent-practice.explain: The amount left over answers this in one step, and comparing it against zero turns a number into the yes-or-no the prompt asked for. The last test catches an over-thought answer: nothing at all splits into any number of equal parts with none over, so `True` is correct there even though it feels like a trick.

independent-practice.prompt: In Python, `"3" + 4` stops the program with a TypeError, but `"3" * 4` runs happily and produces `3333`. Explain why one is refused and the other is not, say what value `"3" * 4` actually is, and describe what you would write instead if you wanted the number seven.
independent-practice.explain: Python refuses `+` between text and a number because there are two plausible meanings - add them, or join them - and guessing wrong would give a silently wrong program instead of a loud one. `*` between text and a whole number has only one plausible meaning, repetition, so it is allowed, and the value it makes is the four-character text `3333` rather than a number in the thousands. Getting seven means converting first, with `int("3") + 4`.

choices: Divides and rounds the answer to the nearest whole number
Divides and discards any fraction, giving the whole part
Divides and always gives a float, exactly like `/`
Marks the rest of the line as a comment
exam.explain: Discarding is not rounding, and the difference shows on `5 // 2`, which is 2 where rounding would give 3. The comment answer is the one carried over from other languages, where `//` starts a comment - in Python that job belongs to `#`.

exam.prompt: What is the difference between `=` and `==`?
choices: There is none; `==` is simply the older spelling
`=` compares two values, and `==` stores a value under a name
`=` stores a value under a name, and `==` asks whether two values are equal
`=` works on numbers and `==` works on text
exam.explain: One is a command that changes the program's state and produces no value; the other is a question that produces `True` or `False` and changes nothing. The swapped answer is worth reading twice, because writing `=` where `==` was meant is precisely the mistake this distinction exists to prevent.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Give all three lines.
exam.explain: Three lines, the same numbers, three different answers - that is precedence and division type in one picture. The third is `7.0` rather than `7` because `/` produces a float and adding a whole number to a float leaves a float; the decimal point is not decoration, it is the type showing itself.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Give both lines.
exam.code:
n = 9
n *= 2
n //= 4
print(n)
n /= 2
print(n)
exam.explain: 18 // 4 is 4, because floor division drops the half rather than rounding it up to 5. The second printed line is `2.0` and not `2`, because `/=` carries the float rule of `/` with it - the same value has changed type without changing much of its size.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Give all three lines.
exam.explain: The first two lines look nearly identical and differ by a factor of thirty-seven, because one repeats a character while the other multiplies a number. The third shows the only way to put a number inside a message at this stage: work the number out, convert it with `str`, then join it.

exam.prompt: Python is evaluating `2 + 12 // 2 ** 2`. Put the three steps into the order it actually performs them.
exam.explain: The power goes first, then the floor division, then the addition - the reverse of reading order, which is why this expression is 5 and not the 8 that working left to right would give. Every wrong ordering here matches a real arithmetic bug somebody has shipped.

exam.prompt:
Give the value `n` refers to after each line runs.

`n = 20`
`n //= 3`
`n += 1`
`n *= 2.0`
exam.explain: 20 // 3 is 6, discarding two thirds rather than rounding up to 7. The final step gives `14.0` and not `14`, because multiplying by a float gives a float even when the answer happens to land on a whole number - the type comes from the operands, not from how the result looks.

exam.prompt: This program should read a whole number typed on one line and print `half: 6` when `13` is typed. Fill the three blanks.
exam.template:
raw = input()
value = ___(raw)
half = value ___ 2
print("half: " + ___(half))
exam.explain: A line typed by a person arrives as text, so it must be converted before it can be divided, and the answer must be converted back before it can be joined to a message - conversion runs in both directions within three lines. `/` in the middle blank would print `half: 6.5`, which the prompt did not ask for.

exam.prompt: This program reads three whole numbers, one per line, and should print their mean. For the typed lines `1`, `2` and `6` it should print `3.0`, but it prints `5.0` instead. Repair it.
exam.starterCode:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
print(a + b + c / 3)
exam.solution:
a = int(input())
b = int(input())
c = int(input())
print((a + b + c) / 3)
exam.explain: Nothing here crashes - the program runs perfectly and prints a confident wrong number, which is what makes precedence bugs expensive to find. Only `c` is being divided, so the repair is brackets around the whole sum, and `/` rather than `//` is right this time because a mean genuinely can be a fraction.

exam.prompt: A shelf holds a fixed number of books. Write a program that reads the total number of books on the first line and the number that fit on one shelf on the second, then prints the number of shelves that end up completely full, then the number of books left over, then `True` if nothing is left over and `False` otherwise - each on its own line. For the typed lines `17` and `5` it prints `3`, then `2`, then `False`.
exam.starterCode:
books = int(input())
per_shelf = int(input())
# three printed lines: full shelves, books left over,
# and whether the books fit exactly
exam.solution:
books = int(input())
per_shelf = int(input())
print(books // per_shelf)
print(books % per_shelf)
print(books % per_shelf == 0)
exam.explain: The third line has to be a question rather than a command, and asking it of the amount left over is cheaper than multiplying the shelves back out and comparing. The third test is the edge worth checking: fewer books than fit on one shelf gives zero full shelves rather than one, which is `//` behaving exactly as it should.
